title: Dark energy may be changing, and 3,000 exploding stars are adding to the mystery
excerpt: Dark energy is the name for whatever pushes the universe apart faster and faster, and the standard picture treats its strength as fixed. At the University of Queensland, astronomers have now rebuilt three decades of exploding stars into one catalog, the largest of its kind.
content:
Dark energy is the name for whatever pushes the universe apart faster and faster, and the standard picture treats its strength as fixed.

At the University of Queensland, astronomers have now rebuilt three decades of exploding stars into one catalog, the largest of its kind.

Set against an unchanging dark energy, the catalog fits worse than before.

The standard model isn’t in trouble yet. But the best record of these explosions anyone has built no longer matches a fixed dark energy comfortably.

Ryan Camilleri, a PhD candidate at UQ’s School of Mathematics and Physics, led the work.

“We’ve rebuilt 3 decades of astronomical observations into a single, consistent framework,” Camilleri said.

Combining decades of data

These explosions are useful because astronomers can use them to measure cosmic distances.

A dead star called a white dwarf detonates, producing an explosion whose brightness can be standardized.

Measure how dim one looks from here, and astronomers can estimate how far away it is.

Astronomers collected them one project at a time. One recent set came from the Dark Energy Survey, which logged 1,635 candidates on its own.

An older and broader set, Pantheon+, drew its measurements from seventeen separate sources, some of them decades old.

Both had the same flaw. They were built by different teams, on different telescopes, with different corrections applied. So one supernova measured twice didn’t always come out the same.

The new catalog, which the team named Unite, runs 2,884 of these explosions through a single pipeline. That makes it the largest and most internally consistent set available.

Older observations were reanalyzed

Camilleri said the team went back over decades of other people’s work with newer knowledge.

“Over the years we’ve learned a lot more about how supernovae behave so we’ve been able to go back and apply that improved understanding to older data.”

Dust makes a supernova look dimmer than it is. So does the mass of the galaxy it exploded in, for reasons astronomers still argue over.

The team re-measured that host mass for more than 98% of the sample, on one consistent scale. And the light itself doesn’t reach Earth in a straight line.

“We also incorporated more subtle effects such as gravitational lensing, which is the bending and magnification of light around large objects as it travels from a supernova to Earth,” Camilleri said.

Unite is the first of these catalogs to correct for that bending by default.

The correction uses how thickly galaxies are packed along the line of sight. Across the more distant half of the sample, it cut the scatter by about 5%.

Fixed dark energy falls short

Einstein’s version of dark energy is a cosmological constant, a fixed property of empty space. Cosmologists write its strength as a number, w, and a true constant means w is exactly −1.

Using Unite alone, the team found w to be −0.764. That is roughly two standard deviations from −1. It’s a gap worth noticing, and not much more.

The direction is the interesting part. Measurements of the leftover light from the Big Bang also disagree with −1, in the opposite direction from the supernovae. One fixed number can’t satisfy both sets at once.

Letting dark energy weaken over time eases that strain. Combined with galaxy maps and the early-universe light, the catalog favors a dark energy that changes as the universe ages.

Camilleri said the combination does not support the standard model.

“Instead of confirming the standard model of cosmology which assumes dark energy is fixed and unchanging, we have more evidence that dark energy may change over time.”

How strong is the evidence?

That is weaker than it sounds, and the authors say so themselves.

By one common measure, the combined data favor changing dark energy at up to 3.3 standard deviations. Physicists call that interesting, well short of proof.

By a second measure, which penalizes the changing model for its extra complexity, the preference is only weak.

About half the error bar on any modern supernova result comes from systematic uncertainty rather than from counting light. Systematic errors aren’t random, which is what statistical tests assume.

Grading a deviation from the standard model with those tests, the authors wrote, is prone to over-interpretation.

Astrophysicist Tamara Davis set the result beside the 2024 survey data that raised the question.

“Our supernova data from DES in 2024 first showed hints that dark energy may be time varying, and this new compilation also sees a deviation from the standard model although in a slightly different direction,” Davis said.

Astronomers running the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument found hints of the same thing in the pattern that relic sound waves left across their 3D map of galaxies.

Supernovae and relic sound waves now point toward evolving dark energy when combined with other cosmological data.

Davis said the answer may reach past cosmology. “All of this research may also hold the clue to explain how gravity and quantum physics fit together.”

Nearby explosions are the weak link

The catalog’s soft spot is close to home. Its nearby supernovae come from many small surveys with mismatched instruments and calibrations.

They also carry outsized weight, because they cover the stretch of cosmic history when dark energy dominates.

Leave out every supernova nearer than a certain distance, and the best fit changes noticeably. That is a lot of influence for the patchiest part of the catalog.

So the honest reading is that a constant fits worse, and the reason isn’t settled. Dark energy may be changing.

Or the nearby explosions may simply be measured less carefully than the far ones. Nothing in Unite tells those two apart.

A survey called DEBASS has already recorded more than 400 supernovae closer to Earth than the Dark Energy Survey reached.

It uses the same telescope and filters as the distant half of this catalog. Folding those in would put the near and far ends of the measurement on one instrument.

The work has not been published in a journal yet. The full paper is available on the preprint server arXiv.
